paper_title: ScaleNav: Scalable Internet Video Pretraining for Language-Conditioned Local Navigation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model's ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Navigating to visible targets according to natural-language instructions is an important capability for robots. For example, person may ask robot to walk to the desk by the window and stop there. Similar instructions also arise in long-horizon systems, where high-level planner, such as an agent based on large language model (LLM), decomposes task into sequence of short-range goals involving visible objects or regions (Huang et al., 2023; Rajvanshi et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2025). We study this language-conditioned local navigation setting: the robot must navigate to text-specified target visible in its initial field of view and stop at the described location. One possible solution is to connect grounding module to an existing navigation method (Shah et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Long et al., 2025; Cerdio et al., 2026), but errors in target grounding and spatial-goal conversion can lead to navigation errors. End-to-end policies provide an alternative by mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to actions (Zhang et al., 2024; Hirose et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Wei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026). To generalize across real-world scenes, these policies require diverse training data (Shah et al., 2023b;c; Sridhar et al., 2024). However, real-robot action data is costly to collect across diverse environments (Liu et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2025), whereas simulated action data still leaves sim-to-real gap (Cai et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026). Internet egocentric videos offer scalable source of visual experience covering diverse real-world scenes and human navigation behavior. However, they lack corresponding robot action labels.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: Overview of ScaleNav. ScaleNav learns navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos through action-free video pretraining, then uses action-labeled simulated data for action alignment and joint fine-tuning. It jointly predicts future observations and action chunks to follow navigation instructions. The right panel illustrates deployment on real quadruped robot. Some methods attempt to leverage these videos by extracting intermediate motion-related supervision, such as estimated trajectories and geometric targets (Cheng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Hirose et al., 2025; Seneviratne et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), or latent actions inferred from visual transitions (Bu et al., 2025). Errors or biases introduced during this extraction can propagate through the resulting supervision into subsequent policy learning. To effectively learn navigation priors from these videos and translate them into executable actions, we propose ScaleNav, framework for language-conditioned local navigation that combines unified world-action model (WAM) with three-stage training procedure. As illustrated in Figure 2, the model uses shared Diffusion Transformer (DiT) (Peebles & Xie, 2023) to jointly predict future observations and action chunks. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on Internet egocentric videos to learn navigation priors from human navigation behavior in diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks while keeping part of the model frozen. Finally, joint fine-tuning optimizes all trainable components together for video and action prediction in navigation. During navigation, the model predicts an action chunk from the instruction and visual observations, executes actions from the chunk, and repeats this process with updated observations until it reaches the target and stops. For evaluation, we construct HabitatGS-LN, benchmark for navigation to specific objects described in natural-language instructions. We also evaluate ScaleNav on single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON (Gong et al., 2026). ScaleNav achieves success rates (SR) of 86.5% on Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on HabitatGS-LN, outperforming the compared methods on both benchmarks. With identical action-labeled simulated data, incorporating Internet egocentric videos improves success by 5.3 and 4.5 percentage points on the two benchmarks, respectively. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on real quadruped robot in three indoor environments. ScaleNav achieves 83.3% overall SR and outperforms the evaluated baselines in all three environments. Our contributions are as follows: We propose ScaleNav, framework for language-conditioned local navigation that transfers navigation priors learned from diverse Internet egocentric videos through video pretraining into executable action chunks via action alignment. Experiments show that ScaleNav outperforms the compared methods in both navigation success rate and path efficiency on the two simulation benchmarks. Real-robot experiments further support ScaleNavs ability to generalize to real-world navigation.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Language-conditioned navigation. Language-conditioned navigation connects language understanding with visual perception, planning, and action generation. Modular approaches combine pretrained foundation models with explicit maps, candidate waypoints, or planning components (Shah et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Long et al., 2025; Cerdio et al., 2026). Learned vision-language-action policies adapt pretrained vision-language backbones to predict navigation actions from instructions and visual observations (Zhang et al., 2024; 2025a; Wei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). Within this direction, dual-system architectures connect high-level semantic reasoning to low-level action generation (Wei et al., 2026; Gong et al., 2026). Within language-conditioned navigation, local navigation focuses on reaching language-specified destination without prescribed route. Methods for this setting learn language-conditioned goal-reaching policies (Hirose et al., 2025; Glossop et al., 2026; Mei et al., 2026) or address local target grounding under occlusion (Gao et al., 2026). We focus on this local navigation setting. World-action models. Using video prediction for robot control requires linking visual predictions to executable actions (Zhao et al., 2026). One approach generates visual plans and recovers actions through inverse dynamics or geometric estimation (Du et al., 2023; Ko et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). Related approaches condition their action decoders on predictive visual features or latents (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a). Another line of work jointly models future observations and actions within unified architecture (Guo et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Cen et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Azuma et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). Following DreamZero, we adopt this joint video-action architecture for navigation. Learning from Internet egocentric videos. Prior work in robot manipulation learns from actionfree human videos through video pretraining (Wu et al., 2024; Cheang et al., 2024) or video-only cross-embodiment transfer (Ye et al., 2026). In navigation, existing approaches leverage these videos mainly in two ways. One line of work uses Internet videos to train navigation policies through intermediate motion-related supervision or latent-action representations. Geometry-based methods derive trajectory or geometric prediction targets from estimated camera motion or reconstructed scenes (Liu et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2026; Han et al., 2025; Seneviratne et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). Other methods obtain action annotations or teacher supervision from learned models (Lin et al., 2023; Hirose et al., 2025). Related video-based methods infer latent actions from visual transitions for policy pretraining (Ye et al., 2025; Bu et al., 2025). Errors or biases in these derived targets and representations can propagate into subsequent policy learning. Another line of work uses Internet videos to learn world models for navigation planning. NWM learns navigation world model from unlabeled videos without proxy motion targets (Bar et al., 2025). Garrido et al. (2026) learn latent-action world model from Internet videos and adapt it to navigation by mapping robot actions to latent actions. These models evaluate candidate trajectories determined by separate search procedure or policy. Better predictions therefore do not necessarily yield better navigation decisions when suitable candidates are missing. Our framework learns navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos and directly predicts executable action chunks, without constructing proxy motion targets for these videos or relying on an external planner at inference.

sections.content: OVERVIEW We study language-conditioned local navigation: given text instruction and stream of RGB observations, robot navigates to target object or region visible in its initial field of view and stops at the instructed location. single action at = (xt, yt, ψt) represents the motion between two consecutive frames, where (xt, yt) is the planar displacement in the robots local coordinates at the preceding frame and ψt is the change in yaw. sequence of actions forms an action chunk, denoted by τ = (a1, . . . , aT ). The robot collects RGB observations while executing each predicted action chunk, then uses the updated observations to predict the next chunk.

Because the two modalities share backbone parameters, action prediction can draw on visual priors learned from Internet egocentric videos. Their noisy counterparts at noise levels tv and ta are denoted by zv ta , respectively. The noisy video and action representations are embedded as tokens, concatenated, and jointly processed by the DiT, conditioned on the navigation instruction l, current observation o, and history. The video and action heads map the corresponding output tokens to flow velocities vv θ for joint denoising, where θ denotes the model parameters. The denoised action representation is denormalized into an action chunk, and the video latents are optionally decoded by the VAE into future observations. tv and za θ and va Initial-frame anchor and recent history. sections.title: 3.2 THREE-STAGE TRAINING
sections.content: We use three-stage training procedure to learn navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos and use them to support action chunk generation. Stage 1 pretrains the model to predict egocentric observations as the camera approaches and reaches the instructed target, conditioned on navigation instructions. Stage 2 introduces action-labeled simulated data for action alignment, learning action prediction with part of the model frozen. Stage 3 jointly fine-tunes the model for video and action prediction. Stage 1: Video pretraining. Pretrained video models provide spatiotemporal priors for action generation (Ye et al., 2026). However, their text conditioning, training-data selection, and prediction schemes differ from the requirements of downstream navigation. First, their text conditions typically describe scene content and motion (Kong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), whereas navigation instructions specify target to reach. Second, during data preparation, camera-dominated footage with little subject motion and clips with pronounced camera shake are sometimes downweighted or excluded (Wan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025), limiting exposure to viewpoint changes and camera shake, both of which are common during robot navigation. Finally, these models commonly generate entire clips bidirectionally (Yang et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2025), whereas navigation requires updating predictions as new observations arrive. To bridge these differences and further learn navigation priors from human navigation in diverse real-world scenes, we continue pretraining Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Wan et al., 2025) on our Internet egocentric videos paired with navigation instructions. To avoid changing the data distribution and prediction structure simultaneously, we first train on these video-instruction pairs using Wans original bidirectional text-image-to-video (TI2V) formulation. Throughout Stage 1, we condition on the navigation instruction and current observation, keeping the observation latent noise-free. We then continue training with chunk-wise prediction, using the initial-frame anchor and recent video chunks as noise-free history, corresponding to the video component of . Chunk-wise causal attention allows current-chunk tokens to attend to historical video tokens while retaining bidirectional attention within the current chunk. In Stages 2 and 3, we also replay Internet egocentric videos from the Stage 1 dataset to help retain the learned video priors, using only the video loss for these samples. In addition, stopping after arrival is an important navigation capability. We model this behavior implicitly through action prediction. Specifically, we pad incomplete final chunks to the fixed length by repeating the last video frame and appending zero-motion actions (0, 0, 0) before action normalization. To avoid potentially disturbing the pretrained video priors with artificially repeated final frames, we exclude latent positions marked as padding from Lvideo by applying temporally max-pooled frame-validity mask. The padded zero actions remain included in Laction to supervise zero-motion outputs after arrival at the target. Stage 3: Joint fine-tuning. Action alignment trains the action modules while keeping much of the video-pretrained model frozen. To further adapt the shared representations to robot navigation together with the action modules, we jointly fine-tune the model. Specifically, we unfreeze the remaining DiT modules and the video head, using the same joint training objective as in Stage 2. 3.3 DATA We construct two datasets for training: action-free Internet egocentric videos and action-labeled simulated data with aligned video and robot actions. Internet egocentric videos. We seek egocentric video clips that capture human navigation behavior across diverse real-world scenes. We use the scene annotations provided by SpatialVIDHQ (Wang et al., 2026a) to select approximately 60K indoor clips from YouTube. For each clip, we provide uniformly sampled keyframes to vision-language model (VLM) to identify candidate endpoints where the camera has arrived near describable object or region. For each candidate endpoint, we take the corresponding object or region as the navigation target and use the VLM to search backward for the earliest keyframe in which the target is visible. Using the selected start and end timestamps, we extract the continuous segment from the source clip. For each extracted segment, we use the VLM to generate navigation instruction describing the target by its category, attributes, or spatial relations. To ensure accurate annotations and plausible navigation behavior, we then review the candidate segments and their instructions using the VLM. After filtering, the Internet egocentric video dataset contains 18.2K navigation segments. Detailed data construction and review procedures are provided in Appendix C. Action-labeled simulated data. To obtain navigation data with aligned video and actions, we generate episodes in Habitat-GS (Xia et al., 2026) using indoor scenes from InteriorGS (Miao et al., 2026). We select targets from the initial observations and use the VLM with scene semantic annotations to generate unambiguous navigation instructions. Using ground-truth navmeshes, we plan smooth, collision-free trajectories with an offline 2D adaptation of SCAN-Planner (Zheng et al., 2026) and collect aligned observations and action labels along these trajectories. We review the resulting samples using criteria similar to those for the Internet egocentric videos, with scene semantic annotations providing additional evidence for instruction accuracy. This yields approximately 2.6K action-labeled episodes from 650 scenes. Further construction details are provided in Appendix C. For both datasets, the VLM paraphrases the instructions of accepted samples to increase language diversity while preserving their meaning.

sections.title: 4.1 SIMULATION EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Benchmarks. We first evaluate on Short-Horizon OVON (Gong et al., 2026), which repositions the starts of HM3D-OVON Val-Unseen episodes (Yokoyama et al., 2024) to the first pose where the target becomes visible. The benchmark was originally developed for three-view setting. We adapt it to our single-view setting, yielding 524 episodes across 36 HM3D scenes (Ramakrishnan et al., 2021), each paired with navigation instruction referring to the target object. Short-Horizon OVON evaluates navigation to category-level goals, but does not explicitly assess whether an agent can identify the intended object from the attributes and spatial relations described in an instruction. To complement this evaluation, we construct HabitatGS-LN, benchmark for language-conditioned local navigation in photorealistic Habitat-GS environments (Xia et al., 2026), with 157 episodes across 45 held-out InteriorGS scenes (Miao et al., 2026). Detailed adaptation and construction procedures are provided in Appendix D. Evaluation protocol. We conduct closed-loop evaluation on Short-Horizon OVON in Habitat (Savva et al., 2019) and on HabitatGS-LN in Habitat-GS (Xia et al., 2026). Episodes terminate according to each methods stopping rule or after 200 execution steps, without using ground-truth target proximity to trigger stopping. Each executed action counts as one step, including each action within predicted chunk. Success requires stopping within the budget and within 1.25 of valid target, measured by the minimum Euclidean distance between their footprints. Valid targets are annotated goal instances of the specified category on Short-Horizon OVON and the instructionspecified instance on HabitatGS-LN. We report success rate (SR), success weighted by path length (SPL) (Anderson et al., 2018), and amortized inference latency per executed action on RTX 4090 GPUs. Profiling and evaluation details are provided in Appendices and D, respectively. Baselines. We compare with NavDP (Cai et al., 2025), ApexNav (Zhang et al., 2025b), StreamVLN (Wei et al., 2025), and Uni-NaVid (Zhang et al., 2025a). To adapt NavDP and ApexNav to our language-conditioned task, we use LocateAnything (Wang et al., 2026c) to ground instruction-specified objects in RGB observations. For NavDP, we back-project the initial detection using simulator-provided ground-truth depth to obtain fixed world-frame goal. We express this goal as 2D vector in the robots current local frame at each step. For ApexNav, LocateAnything replaces the detectors in its category-level query pipeline. Both methods receive ground-truth depth with maximum ranges of 5 for NavDP and 4.99 for ApexNav, following their original evaluation settings. For StreamVLN and Uni-NaVid, we evaluate both released checkpoints and versions fine-tuned on our action-labeled simulated data. Fine-tuning uses no additional DAgger (Ross et al., 2011) rollouts or reinforcement learning. Adaptation and fine-tuning details are provided in Appendix D. We also evaluate variant without additional training on our Internet egocentric videos. This variant skips Stage 1 and starts directly from the pretrained Wan weights, retaining Stages 2 and 3 on actionlabeled simulated data but omitting video replay. Comparative results. As shown in Table 1, ScaleNav outperforms the evaluated baselines in SR and SPL on both benchmarks. Compared with our variant without Internet egocentric videos, SR improves by 5.3 and 4.5 percentage points on Short-Horizon OVON and HabitatGS-LN, respectively. These gains support the benefit of learning navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos. Our framework also achieves comparatively low amortized inference latency of 76 ms per executed action. 4.2 ABLATION STUDIES We conduct the following ablation studies on HabitatGS-LN. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented ScaleNav, language-conditioned local navigation framework that learns navigation priors through Internet egocentric video pretraining and translates them into executable action chunks through action alignment and joint fine-tuning. Simulation experiments demonstrate the benefits of Internet egocentric videos and improvements over the evaluated baselines in success rate and path efficiency. Real-robot experiments further support generalization to real-world navigation. For limitations, our quantitative evaluation focuses on indoor navigation to initially visible object

sections.content: Model and input configuration. We use RGB frames at resolution of 512 288 pixels and sampling rate of 4 Hz. Each video chunk contains nine observations, oi, . . . , oi+8, with oi Its = 9 actions correspond to the transitions serving as the current-observation condition. oi oi+1, . . . , oi+8 oi+9, where oi+9 is the first observation of the next chunk. The VAE encodes the nine frames into three temporal latent slices. The history window retains the two most recent chunks in addition to the initial-frame anchor. Each action component is normalized using scaled symlog transformation (Hafner et al., 2025), (u) = sign(u) log(1 + u/c), with = 0.01 for translation and = 0.01 rad for yaw. We recover action components using 1(z) = sign(z)(exp(z) 1). Training configuration. We use AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with BF16 mixed precision throughout training. Table 4 summarizes the stage-specific settings. Video pretraining consists of 2,000 updates under the original video-training formulation, followed by 8,000 updates with chunk-wise causal prediction. For joint fine-tuning, we warm up the learning rate over 500 updates, hold it constant until update 4,000, and apply cosine decay to 5 107 by update 5,500. It remains constant thereafter, and we use the checkpoint at update 6,500 for evaluation. Inference and execution. We jointly generate video latents and action chunks using four Euler denoising steps. The classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022) scales are 5.0 for video and 1.0 for actions, with noise-schedule shift factors of 5.0 and 1.0, respectively. At each denoising step, the model receives the video and action noise levels from their respective schedules, and each modality is updated using its own Euler step size. The unconditional branch removes the text condition while retaining the current observation and history. During simulation evaluation, we execute the nine actions in each chunk sequentially at 4 Hz and predict the next chunk from the latest observation, unless the episode terminates. During simulation evaluation, action history stores the models previous action predictions rather than measured robot displacements. Inference optimizations. Historical tokens use fixed zero-noise timesteps and cannot attend to the current chunk. We therefore compute their keys and values once for each classifier-free guidance branch and reuse them across denoising steps (Ye et al., 2026). We batch the conditional and unconditional forward passes for classifier-free guidance and use CUDA graphs1 to reduce kernel-launch overhead. We also omit RGB decoding of the predicted video latents because action execution does not require the generated frames. At four denoising steps, these optimizations reduce per-chunk policy-call latency from 1,791 to 684 ms, 2.6 speedup  (Table 5)  . The step-count sweep measures latency only, not navigation success. We profile ScaleNav on recorded observations in BF16 using CUDA synchronization and the guidance settings above. Table 5 reports mean per-chunk policy-call latency, including currentobservation encoding, completed-chunk history encoding, history KV prefill, denoising, and buffered-action retrieval. Video decoding is included only in the ablation configurations that retain it. Measurements exclude simulator rendering, network communication, and motion execution. The four-step configurations use 23 measured chunks after five warm-up chunks per configuration. Configurations with more denoising steps use 10 measured chunks after four warm-up chunks. The segment-review prompt below assesses target-instruction consistency, motion plausibility, arrival accuracy, and temporal continuity. We separately label the candidate segment and the surrounding endpoint context to support arrival assessment. Review the candidate navigation segment and its instruction. Inputs: - Instruction: {instruction} - Target description: {target_description} - Segment boundaries: {start_frame}, {end_frame} - Chronologically ordered frames covering the segment. - Separately labeled source frames around the candidate endpoint. Assess the following four criteria: 1. Target-instruction consistency: Verify that the initial and final frames depict the same target and that its category and visible attributes match the instruction. Check that any stated spatial relations are supported by the initial observation, using that view as the reference for left/right and ordinal descriptions. When multiple plausible targets are visible, verify that the instruction uniquely identifies the intended target. Mark this criterion as "fail" if the wording is ambiguous, or "uncertain" if the visual evidence is insufficient to decide. 2. Motion plausibility: Check that the segment primarily shows camera movement toward the target, rather than prolonged in-place rotation, stationary observation, or back-and-forth motion that does not advance toward it. 3. Arrival accuracy: Examine the frames around the candidate endpoint to determine whether the camera has reached the target's vicinity. 4. Temporal continuity: Check for scene cuts or abrupt temporal jumps within the selected segment. Return JSON with the keys "target_instruction_consistency", "motion_plausibility", "arrival_accuracy", and "temporal_continuity". For each criterion, provide "decision" ("pass", "fail", or "uncertain") and brief "reason" grounded in the supplied frames. Include "keep", set to true only when all four criteria pass. sections.title: D BENCHMARK AND EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: Single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON. To adapt Short-Horizon OVON (Gong et al., 2026) to our single-view setting, we retain episodes with an estimated target visibility of at least 50% in the initial front view. We estimate visibility as the fraction of sampled vertices from the targets semantic mesh (Yadav et al., 2023) whose projections fall within the same instances region in the initial front-view semantic image. This is target-visibility fraction, not the fraction of image pixels occupied by the target. The resulting evaluation set contains 524 episodes across 36 HM3D scenes (Ramakrishnan et al., 2021), each paired with navigation instruction referring to the target object. Because this evaluation uses our single-view selection and the shared protocol in Section 4.1, its results are not directly comparable to results under the original three-view protocol. HabitatGS-LN construction. We use indoor scenes from InteriorGS (Miao et al., 2026) that are held out from training. Their scene IDs are disjoint from those of the 650 scenes used for our 2,600 action-labeled simulated training episodes. Using the simulation pipeline described in Section 3.3, we generate candidate episodes covering diverse object categories and spatial descriptions. Each episode specifies an initial robot pose and navigation instruction that unambiguously refers to specific object visible in the initial observation, rather than an object category. Although our task formulation allows both object and region targets, we restrict this benchmark to object targets for comparison with baselines designed for object-goal navigation. Human review. To ensure the quality and validity of the evaluation tasks, two human reviewers independently inspect each candidate episode. They assess instruction accuracy and clarity, target visibility in the initial observation, destination reachability, and scene rendering quality. We retain only episodes approved by both reviewers, yielding 157 episodes across 45 scenes. Figure 6 shows example tasks from HabitatGS-LN.

Figure 6: Example tasks in HabitatGS-LN with their final navigation instructions. Red boxes mark the specified targets. Simulation camera configuration. For all methods on both simulation benchmarks, we render RGB observations at resolution of 512288 pixels with horizontal field of view of approximately 70. Simulation action execution. In both environments, we conduct closed-loop evaluation by executing the predicted actions and updating observations as the robot moves. We convert each methods discrete or continuous action outputs into kinematic pose updates. Within each scene, all methods use the same navmesh-based motion constraints. NavDP goal construction. We compute the median of the valid depth values within the detected bounding box and select the pixel whose depth is closest to this median. Using its depth, the camera intrinsics, and the simulator-provided camera pose, we back-project this pixel into world coordinates without snapping the resulting point to the navmesh. We keep this world-frame goal fixed and express it as 2D vector in the robots current local frame at each step. NavDP predicts motion trajectories conditioned on this local goal and RGB-D observations. ApexNav adaptation. ApexNavs original detection pipeline uses category-level queries. We replace YOLOv7 (Wang et al., 2023) and Grounding DINO (Liu et al., 2024) with LocateAnything to process the referring expressions in our instructions. The resulting detections feed into its segmentation, semantic fusion, and navigation pipeline. Baseline fine-tuning. We prepare fine-tuning data for StreamVLN and Uni-NaVid from our action-labeled simulated training episodes. path follower converts the reference trajectories into each models native discrete actions. We execute these actions in Habitat-GS and re-render observations at the corresponding poses to ensure alignment between the visual observations and discrete action labels. We confirmed that all trajectories used for fine-tuning terminated near their intended goals. The resulting observation-action sequences are then paired with the navigation instructions and formatted for each model. We adopt the optimization hyperparameters from StreamVLNs Stage 1 training script and UniNaVids Stage 2 fine-tuning script. We initialize both models from their released checkpoints and fine-tune each model for five epochs using AdamW with global batch size of 128. StreamVLN uses base learning rate of 2105 and learning rate of 5106 for its vision encoder. Uni-NaVid uses learning rate of 105 and keeps its vision encoder frozen. Footprint distance. The robot and target footprints are the regions they occupy when projected onto the ground plane. We model the robot footprint as an oriented capsule with radius of 0.25 and centerline length of 0.36 m, using SCAN-Planners Go2 parameters (Zheng et al., 2026). We measure the minimum Euclidean distance between this capsule and the targets annotated groundplane polygon (Ericson, 2004).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: SPL reference lengths. We compute reference lengths as the shortest navmesh distances to annotated goal positions on HabitatGS-LN and to sampled navigable points near valid target footprints on Short-Horizon OVON. Stopping rules. Our model stops when five consecutive actions have translation magnitudes below 0.015 and absolute yaw changes below 0.015 rad. NavDP stops when the robot is within 1 of its estimated goal point on the ground plane. For the remaining baselines, we retain their default stopping mechanisms: explicit STOP actions for StreamVLN and Uni-NaVid, and rule-based stopping for ApexNav. Pseudo-action labeling ablation. We use Depth Anything 3 (DA3-Nested) (Lin et al., 2026) to estimate metric camera poses from Internet egocentric videos. We invert the predicted world-tocamera transforms to obtain camera-to-world poses. We then express consecutive relative motions in camera-aligned planar frame to obtain pseudo action labels. We retain clips with available pose estimates and do not apply confidence-based loss weighting.
